title: Dolma yaprak
subtitle: Vine leaves stuffed with rice, lamb, and spices
excerpt: Dolma yaprak are Turkish stuffed vine leaves filled with rice, lamb mince, pine nuts, currants, and warm spices, then poached in a lemony stock until tender. They take patience to roll but the process is meditative and the result is deeply good. Serve warm or at room temperature with yoghurt.
sourceNotes: Stuffed vine leaves appear across Turkey, Greece, Lebanon, and the wider Middle Eastern region. The Turkish version often includes pine nuts and currants in the filling, giving it a sweet-savoury quality.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze after cooking. Defrost and reheat gently in a covered pan.
recipe.batchNotes: The recipe scales up easily. Make a double batch if you have a big pot.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made a day ahead. The rolls firm up in the fridge and the flavour deepens.

content.text: Stuffed vine leaves are one of the most rewarding things you can make. The rolling takes time but quickly becomes rhythmic, and the result is a pot of neat, aromatic parcels that taste nothing like the tinned version.

The Turkish filling with pine nuts and currants adds a sweet note that plays off the slightly tart vine leaves. The rice is added raw and absorbs the cooking liquid, so the filling stays juicy rather than drying out.

Jarred vine leaves in brine need a quick rinse and blanch in boiling water for a minute or two to soften them. Lay out a good batch and work through them assembly-line style to keep the process moving.

items.prepNote: jarred in brine, rinsed and blanched for 2 minutes

content.text: Warm the olive oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 6 minutes until soft. Add the lamb mince and break it up, cooking for 5 minutes until browned. Remove from the heat. Stir in the rice, pine nuts, raisins, spices, mint, parsley, and salt. Mix well.

Lay a vine leaf flat, shiny side down. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre near the stem end. Fold the bottom up over the filling, fold in the sides, and roll up tightly towards the tip. Do not roll too loosely; the rice will expand. Layer torn or torn-up vine leaves over the base of the casserole to prevent sticking. Pack the rolls tightly in the pot, seam side down, in compact layers.

Mix the stock, olive oil, and lemon juice together and pour over the stuffed rolls. The liquid should come to just below the top layer. Place a heatproof plate directly on top of the rolls to hold them in place. Cover the pot and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook over a low heat for 50 to 55 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid absorbed. Rest for 10 minutes before uncovering.

rows.cause: Too little liquid or cooked at too low a heat
rows.fix: Add 100 ml of hot water, replace the plate and lid, and cook for a further 15 minutes over a slightly higher heat.

rows.cause: Rolls not packed tightly enough or plate not used
rows.fix: Pack them as tightly as possible and always use a plate to weigh them down; it prevents them moving and opening.
Blanch for 2 to 3 minutes in boiling water; they should feel pliable and soft before rolling.

content.text: For a meatless version, omit the lamb and increase the pine nuts and use vegetable stock instead. These are served cold in Turkish mezze and are made slightly more lemony. Fresh dill can replace the parsley for a different herbal note.
Dolma yaprak are best made a day ahead. Refrigerate after cooking; the rolls firm up and the flavour deepens. Reheat gently or serve at room temperature.

Stuffed vine leaves are shared across Turkey, Greece, Lebanon, Syria, Iran, and much of the wider region. The Turkish version is typically served warm as a main course with yoghurt. The cold oil-and-herb version is a mezze staple in Greek and Lebanese kitchens.
